chapter_theme: Impatience for reunion on both sides of the distance. She has worn down her fingers counting days and rehearses how she will greet him, and, on Parimelazhagar's reading, he is stuck on campaign and starting to fear he may come back too late.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1261-1267 to the woman and 1268-1270 to the man, arguing against earlier commentators who give 1268 to the woman. Manakkudavar does give 1268 and 1270 to the woman.

1261.reading: The woman says her eyes have lost their light and her fingers have worn down from marking the days since he left.
1261.nuance: Fingers wear down from touching marks on a wall, in Parimelazhagar's and Kalaignar's picture, and from folding to count, in Manakkudavar's. The verse itself just says they marked the days. Either way, this is the book's most concrete image of waiting.

1262.reading: The woman tells her bright-jewelled friend that if she forgets him today, her beauty will leave and the bangles will slip from her shoulders thereafter.

positions.position: 'Today' is the day of her death and மேல் is the next birth: remembering him at the moment of death is how she can reach him in the next life.
positions.quote: இவ்வெல்லைக்கண் நினைந்தால் மறுமைக்கண் அவரை எய்தி அன்புறலாம்;

positions.position: The verse is about this life: if she forgets, her body will fail, and the address means 'you who have no pain'.
positions.quote: தம்மழகினை நீக்கி வளை முதலான அணிகலங்களையும் கழலவிடும்

1263.reading: The woman says she still lives by longing for the return of the man who left, longing for victory, with his own resolve as his companion.
1263.nuance: The pointed word is துணை, 'companion'. Parimelazhagar spells it out: he has scorned her as a partner and taken resolve instead. There are two longings set side by side, நசைஇ in each line, for victory and for him.

1264.reading: The woman says that thinking of the return of the man who left with the love they shared, her heart கோடுகொடேறும்.

positions.position: The heart puts out branches, swelling and rising as a tree does, with sorrow gone.
The heart climbs a tree to look for him, because from the top one can see someone coming from afar.

1265.reading: The woman says may she see her husband till her eyes are full, and after that the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave.
1265.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes what this is answering: the friend brings news that he's coming, and asks why she still pales. Her answer is that hearing won't do it, since the eyes must see. The news of the cure isn't the cure.

1266.reading: The woman says may her husband come one day, and she'll drink him in so that all this agonising sickness is destroyed.
1266.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes பருகுவன் drinking through all five senses, recalling 1101, and says that in that single day she'll destroy not only all past pain but all that might still come. That one day is asked to carry a lot.

1267.reading: The woman asks, should he who is dear as her eyes return, whether she will sulk, embrace him or do both.
1267.nuance: The chapter's real interest here is the planning, with him not yet home. Parimelazhagar sets aside an alternative, that the third means to behave as if nothing happened: she wants to do all three, and that's her impatience.

1268.reading: Let the king fight and win, and let there be a home-joined feast for the evening; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
1268.nuance: Parimelazhagar rejects the woman's reading at length, on the grounds that she wouldn't name the king rather than the husband. But Manakkudavar gives a reason for that: the king's unfinished war is what holds him back. Evening, the woman's executioner, is for the man a feast to come.

positions.position: The man, stuck on campaign, says to himself that he wants to join his wife; மனை here stands for the wife.
positions.quote: வேந்தற்கு உற்றுழிப் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் வினை முடிவு நீட்டித் துழித் தலைமகளை நினைந்து தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது.

positions.position: The woman speaks: let the king win, and I will prepare a feast at home, with மனை meaning the kitchen.
The man speaks: if the leader wins, he will feast with his wife.

1269.reading: One day passes like seven for those who pine with an eye on the day when those far away return; Parimelazhagar gives it to the man, projecting her pain, and the other commentators name no speaker.
1269.nuance: Parimelazhagar uses the general phrasing as proof that it can't be the woman: she would say 'me', so the man is imagining how it is for her. If he's right, it's a rare moment in the book when a man grasps the other side of his absence. He takes 'seven' as meaning many.

1270.reading: What use is it if she gets, or has got, or even touches, once the heart has broken and spilled? The speaker is the man, of her, for Parimelazhagar, and the woman, of herself, for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The man fears that she may die before he gets back, and it can't be her voice, since then it would be a lament and not impatience.
positions.quote: இது தலைமகள் கூற்றாயவழி இரங்கலாவதல்லது விதுப்பாகாமை அறிக.

positions.position: The woman answers the friend who says that he will come: what use, if my own heart has already broken?
positions.quote: இது வருவா ரென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் கூறியது.

links.note: 1151 tells him to bring promises of quick return to those who will still be alive. 1270, in Parimelazhagar's reading, has the man finally arriving at that thought himself, from the other end of the journey and perhaps too late. The warning was given at the start of the separation, and he feels it only at the end.

591 says ஊக்கம், inner resolve, is the only true possession. In 1263, the woman names a very similar quality in உள்ளம் as his companion in leaving her. The virtue the Book of Wealth values most is what she has been left for.

If Parimelazhagar's speaker is correct, evening is a coming feast for the man in 1268, and for the woman in 1224 it comes like a killer to the execution ground. They are thinking about the same hour, far apart, and with opposite expectations.

1267 is a plan: sulk, embrace or both. 1259 records how such a plan works out: she goes to sulk, and her heart gives way. The planner in 1267 hasn't learned anything from the experience, or she has and enjoys planning anyway.

source_issues: 1261: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts mid-gloss, without a headnote.
1267: The verse text has விரன் where the commentators and meaning require வரின். Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is the same as Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1268: Pope's prose has 'my wife', while his couplet is unclear about the speaker.
